blocks.text: Two welders join the same 20 mm steel plate with the same electrode. One travels briskly and leaves a narrow bead; the other crawls and leaves a wide, heavy one. Years later the slow weld cracks in service while the fast one does not. The difference is the heat each put into every millimetre of joint, which sets how fast the metal around the weld cooled.

blocks.markdown: In arc welding the arc converts electrical power into heat at the workpiece. Not all of it enters the plate: some is lost to radiation, spatter and the shielding gas. The fraction that enters is the **arc efficiency** $\eta$. The arc power is voltage times current ($VI$, in W), and the heat delivered per unit length of weld depends on how quickly the arc moves along the joint. This is the **heat input**, and it is the single most useful number for predicting what a welding procedure does to the metal.

blocks.title: Arc welding heat input
blocks.text: Heat input per unit length is $H=\eta VI/v$, where $V$ is arc voltage (V), $I$ is welding current (A), $v$ is travel speed (mm/s) and $\eta$ is arc efficiency (dimensionless). With these units $H$ is in J/mm; divide by 1000 for kJ/mm. Typical efficiencies (representative values, which depend on the standard used) are about 0.8 for MMA and MAG, 0.6 for TIG and 1.0 for submerged arc.

blocks.caption: Heat input per unit length; a travel speed given in mm/min must first be divided by 60

blocks.title: Heat input for a MAG weld
blocks.prompt: A MAG weld is made at $V=24$ V and $I=220$ A with travel speed 240 mm/min. Take $\eta=0.8$. Find the heat input.
blocks.answer: The heat input is 1056 J/mm, or 1.06 kJ/mm.

blocks.markdown: The heat flows into the plate by conduction. Near the arc the metal is above its melting point, and as the arc moves on, the heat spreads outward into the cold plate and the weld cools. For a thick plate, where heat flows in three dimensions, an analysis of a moving point source (Rosenthal) gives the cooling rate at the weld centreline at a temperature $T_c$ in terms of the heat input, the plate's initial temperature $T_0$ and the thermal conductivity $k$. The key result is that the cooling rate is inversely proportional to the heat input.

blocks.caption: Cooling rate at $T_c$ for a thick plate ($R$ in $^\circ$C/s, $k$ in W/(mm K), $H$ in J/mm); typical $k\approx0.028$ W/(mm K) for carbon steel

blocks.title: Cooling rate in a thick steel plate
blocks.prompt: For the weld above ($H=1056$ J/mm) in thick carbon steel starting at $T_0=20^\circ$C, estimate the cooling rate at $T_c=550^\circ$C using $k=0.028$ W/(mm K).
blocks.answer: The cooling rate is about 47 degrees C per second; doubling the heat input would halve it to 23.

blocks.markdown: A weld cross-section etched for macro examination shows three regions. The **fusion zone** (weld metal) is the metal that melted and re-solidified, with a cast, columnar structure whose composition is a mixture of filler and melted parent metal. Beyond the **fusion line** lies the **heat-affected zone (HAZ)**, base metal that did not melt but was heated enough for its microstructure and properties to change. Further out is the unaffected **parent metal**, whose properties are those of the original plate.

rows: Melted and re-solidified, columnar cast structure
About 1100 $^\circ$C up to the fusion line
Large austenite grains, can transform to hard brittle martensite or bainite on fast cooling
blocks.caption: Zones across a weld in carbon steel (approximate temperatures; they depend on the steel)

blocks.markdown: Heat input controls the width of the HAZ and its microstructure. High heat input and slow travel means a slow cooling rate: the metal spends longer at high temperature, grains grow, and the coarse-grained HAZ is wider with lower toughness. Low heat input (fast travel, low current) gives fast cooling, which suppresses grain growth but promotes hard, brittle martensite in hardenable steels and raises the risk of cracking. Welding procedures aim for a heat input window between these extremes.

blocks.title: Heat input and cooling rate are inversely related
blocks.text: $R\propto1/H$ for a given plate and preheat. Faster travel, lower current or higher preheat each changes the cooling rate in a predictable direction, so the heat input is the main control variable.

blocks.title: Units
blocks.text: Convert travel speed to mm/s before using $H=\eta VI/v$, and check whether the efficiency has already been included in the quoted heat input. Cooling-rate formulas such as the one above also assume a particular plate thickness regime (thick plate).

points: Heat input is $H=\eta VI/v$; typical $\eta$ is about 0.8 for MAG and MMA, 0.6 for TIG and 1.0 for submerged arc.
Thick-plate cooling rate at a given temperature is $R=2\pi k(T_c-T_0)^2/H$, inversely proportional to heat input.
High heat input gives slow cooling, a wider HAZ and coarser grain; low heat input gives fast cooling and a risk of hard brittle microstructure.
A weld section shows fusion zone, HAZ (melted-and-changed, unmelted-but-changed) and unaffected parent metal.

questions.stem: In a macro-section of a fusion weld in steel, which region is the metal that was melted and re-solidified?

options.text: The heat-affected zone
The fusion zone
The parent metal
The fusion line only

distractorRationale.a: The HAZ is base metal that did not melt, though its microstructure was changed by heating.
distractorRationale.c: The parent metal is far enough away that it was not significantly heated.
distractorRationale.d: The fusion line is the boundary between melted and unmelted metal, not the whole melted region.

questions.explanation: The fusion zone is the weld metal that reached its melting point and re-solidified. The HAZ lies just outside it and was heated enough to change structure without melting.

questions.stem: A GMAW weld is made at 28 V and 300 A with a travel speed of 360 mm/min and arc efficiency 0.8. Calculate the heat input per unit length in kJ/mm.
questions.explanation: The speed is $360/60=6$ mm/s. Then $H=0.8\times28\times300/6=1120$ J/mm, i.e. 1.12 kJ/mm.

questions.stem: A manual metal arc electrode run of 150 mm takes 45 s to deposit at 23 V and 180 A. Taking arc efficiency 0.75, calculate the heat input in kJ/mm.
questions.explanation: The travel speed is $150/45=3.333$ mm/s. Then $H=\eta VI/v=0.75\times23\times180/3.333=932$ J/mm, or 0.93 kJ/mm.

questions.stem: The travel speed of a weld is doubled with voltage, current and efficiency unchanged. What happens to the heat input per unit length and to the cooling rate (thick plate)?

options.text: Heat input doubles and cooling rate halves
Heat input is unchanged and cooling rate is unchanged
Heat input halves and cooling rate halves
Heat input halves and cooling rate roughly doubles

questions.correctOptionText: Heat input halves and cooling rate roughly doubles

distractorRationale.a: This is the reverse; faster travel gives less heat per length.
distractorRationale.b: Heat input depends on $1/v$, so it must change.
distractorRationale.c: Cooling rate is inversely proportional to heat input, so it moves opposite to it.

questions.explanation: Since $H=\eta VI/v$, doubling $v$ halves $H$. The thick-plate cooling rate $R=2\pi k(T_c-T_0)^2/H$ is inversely proportional to $H$ so it roughly doubles.

questions.stem: A weld in thick carbon steel plate initially at 20 $^\circ$C has heat input 1500 J/mm. Use $R=2\pi k(T_c-T_0)^2/H$ with $k=0.028$ W/(mm K) to find the cooling rate at 550 $^\circ$C, in $^\circ$C/s.
questions.explanation: The temperature difference is $530\,^\circ$C, so $R=2\pi(0.028)(530)^2/1500=49419/1500=32.9$ $^\circ$C/s. A higher heat input than the previous example gives a lower cooling rate.

questions.stem: A fabricator reduces welding speed to deposit a larger bead on 25 mm steel plate, increasing heat input substantially. What is the most likely metallurgical consequence in the heat-affected zone?

options.text: A wider HAZ with coarser grain and lower toughness
A narrower HAZ with finer grain
No change, since arc power is unchanged
Higher hardness because of faster cooling

questions.correctOptionText: A wider HAZ with coarser grain and lower toughness

distractorRationale.b: A narrow HAZ comes from low heat input and fast travel, not the reverse.
distractorRationale.c: Power may be unchanged but heat per length rises with lower speed, so the HAZ changes.
distractorRationale.d: Slow cooling reduces hardness; fast cooling is what increases it.

questions.explanation: Higher heat input means a slower cooling rate and a longer time at high temperature. This lets austenite grains grow and widens the HAZ, usually reducing toughness.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the heat-affected zone?

options.text: Metal that melted and solidified
Filler metal added to the joint
Parent metal that did not melt but whose microstructure was altered by welding heat
Metal ahead of the arc that is unaffected by heat

questions.correctOptionText: Parent metal that did not melt but whose microstructure was altered by welding heat

distractorRationale.a: This describes the fusion zone, not the HAZ.
distractorRationale.b: Filler metal is melted and becomes part of the fusion zone.
distractorRationale.d: Metal far from the weld is the unaffected parent metal.

questions.explanation: The HAZ is the base metal outside the fusion line that was raised to a high enough temperature to change its structure and properties but not to melt. It therefore sits between the melted fusion zone and the unaffected parent metal.

questions.stem: A macro-section of a steel weld shows, moving outward from the weld centre: columnar grains, then a band of very coarse grains, then fine grains, then unchanged parent plate. Which statement best identifies the zones and the likely weakest HAZ band?

options.text: Parent metal, fine-grained HAZ, coarse-grained HAZ, fusion zone
Fusion zone, fine-grained HAZ, coarse-grained HAZ, parent metal
HAZ, fusion zone, coarse-grained HAZ, parent metal
Fusion zone, coarse-grained HAZ (typically the lowest toughness), fine-grained HAZ, parent metal

questions.correctOptionText: Fusion zone, coarse-grained HAZ (typically the lowest toughness), fine-grained HAZ, parent metal

distractorRationale.a: This reverses the order; the fusion zone is at the weld centre.
distractorRationale.b: The coarse-grained HAZ is closest to the fusion line (highest peak temperature), not beyond the fine-grained region.
distractorRationale.c: The HAZ is outside, not inside, the fusion zone.

questions.explanation: Peak temperature falls with distance from the weld centre: melted fusion zone, then coarse-grained HAZ next to the fusion line, then refined grain, then parent metal. The coarse-grained region is usually the toughness-critical zone.

questions.stem: Explain why increasing the heat input of an arc weld produces a wider heat-affected zone with coarser grains, and why very low heat input can also be harmful in a hardenable steel.
markingGuide: Heat input $H=\eta VI/v$; larger $H$ means slower cooling
Slow cooling gives more time at high temperature so grains grow and the HAZ widens
Low heat input gives fast cooling, promoting hard brittle martensite in hardenable steel
Cracking risk increases; a heat input window or preheat is used
questions.explanation: Higher heat input slows cooling, so grains grow and the HAZ is wider. Very low heat input cools so fast in hardenable steel that martensite forms, which can crack.

questions.stem: A TIG weld and a submerged-arc weld are made with the same voltage, current and travel speed on the same plate. Compare their heat inputs using typical arc efficiencies, and describe how the difference would show in the cross-section and cooling rate.
markingGuide: $H=\eta VI/v$ with $\eta\approx0.6$ for TIG and about 1.0 for submerged arc (typical values)
SAW heat input is about 1.7 times higher with identical $V$, $I$, $v$
Higher heat input gives a larger fusion zone and wider HAZ for SAW
Slower cooling rate (inversely proportional to $H$) for SAW
Identify fusion zone, HAZ and parent metal in the section
questions.explanation: Because $\eta$ differs, the SAW weld puts about 1.0/0.6 times more heat into each millimetre. It therefore has a bigger weld pool, wider HAZ and slower cooling.
